source.title: Equivariant Transformer is all you need

record.file_problem: The paper text is present, but Figure 4's plotted data are not available in the supplied text, only its caption.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a scaling relationship in a new setting: an equivariant Transformer used for a lattice-physics model, rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports MSE versus trainable parameters in Figure 4 and explicitly says the model shows a scaling law. The supplied text does not provide plotted values or establish that the relationship has the same power-law form as the claim. Acceptance-rate results versus layer count are not rows because they do not measure the loss scaling named in the claim.
record.test_reason: The paper fits MSE against trainable parameters for equivariant Transformers with 2 to 6 layers in a lattice spin-fermion Monte Carlo setting. It explicitly frames the result as the Kaplan-style power-type scaling law, which bears on V5 in a new, non-language setting. Evidence is figure-only and comes from a short proceedings paper.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the loss (MSE) is estimated from the acceptance ratio. The abstract describes the result as a scaling law 'of the acceptance rate', while the body describes a scaling law of the loss with trainable parameters.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a lattice-physics model and MSE estimated from acceptance, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy; plots MSE against trainable parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: SLMC acceptance rate rises with the number of attention layers, from 21% for the linear model (Fig. 4 left). The abstract calls this a 'scaling law of the acceptance rate'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sampler acceptance rate improves monotonically with effective-model depth.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of The 40th International Symposium on Lattice Field Theory — PoS(LATTICE2023)
record.problems: The supplied text gives no plotted MSE or parameter values, fit coefficients, or uncertainty estimates for Figure 4, and does not explicitly characterize the reported relationship as a power law.
record.rows_left_out: The acceptance-rate-versus-layer-count result in Figure 4, left panel, was left out because it does not measure the loss scaling named in the claim.

untested.parts: Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer settings. Scaling in data or compute rather than parameters. Any explicit exponent or confirmation of power-law form, since the text gives no fit form or coefficients.
Extrapolation to much larger runs; not studied.
Shape at fixed parameter count; not studied.

missing.what: The fitted scaling relation itself: MSE vs trainable parameters across L=2–6, including fit form, exponent and parameter range. Only the per-point rows exist.
missing.locator: Figure 4 right panel and caption; Section 4 final paragraph

record.verdict_notes: Evidence is weak: a proceedings paper with figure-only data and no stated exponent, coefficients or uncertainties. Each layer has about 3×(Ñ+1)=21 attention weights, so total parameters likely span well under one order of magnitude; this is my inference from Eqs. 4–7. The 'loss' is derived from acceptance rate, not held-out cross-entropy.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute changes.
Loss comparisons across architectures at fixed parameter count.

Tests only MSE versus trainable parameters for a lattice-physics model. It does not test other modalities such as image or video, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or whether the relationship matches the same power-law form.
Downstream task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices, or whether curves depart from a single power law.

relationships.condition: Equivariant Transformer effective models with L=2–6 layers in SLMC on a 6×6 double-exchange lattice
relationships.reason: Based on the text, since rows r3–r7 are figure-only. The authors state the model 'shows the scaling law', citing Kaplan's power-type law, with a fit over L=2–6.
relationships.display_finding: The effective models followed a reported Kaplan-type power law over depths of 2–6 layers.

relationships.reason: The caption says the fit excludes L=1 (r2), so the law is reported to hold only beyond the smallest model. The parameter range is also very narrow (a few to roughly a hundred-odd parameters, inferred from the architecture).
relationships.display_finding: The fit excluded L = 1 and covered only a narrow parameter range, approximately a few to a hundred-odd parameters inferred from the architecture.
